n: The second Servant Song. The Servant speaks to distant peoples: God called him before birth and named him. Nephi quotes this chapter as 1 Nephi 21, adding an opening address to scattered Israel, “broken off” because of wicked pastors—which fits Lehi’s family.

f.g: Nephi taught that his people lived on an “isle of the sea.”

f.w: The LORD hath called me from the womb

n: God made the Servant’s words sharp like a sword and kept him hidden like a polished arrow in a quiver, ready for the right moment.

f.w: my mouth like a sharp sword

n: God calls the Servant “Israel,” in whom He will be glorified. The Servant embodies what Israel was meant to be—ultimately fulfilled in Christ, and also in faithful covenant Israel.

f.w: Thou art my servant, O Israel

n: The Servant feels his work has failed—spent for nothing. Yet he trusts that God will judge and reward him. A comforting verse for anyone who feels their efforts haven’t mattered.

f.w: my judgment is with the LORD
f.g: My cause and my reward are in God’s hands.

n: God formed the Servant to bring Jacob back to Him. Even if Israel doesn’t gather at first, the Servant is honored by God, who is his strength.

f.g: Some manuscripts read “that Israel might be gathered to him.”

n: Restoring Israel is too small a task; God will also make the Servant a light to the Gentiles, bringing salvation to the ends of the earth. Paul and Barnabas cited this verse as their mission to the Gentiles.

The Servant is despised by people and nations, a servant of rulers—yet kings will rise and princes bow because the faithful Lord has chosen him. This anticipates the rejected yet exalted Messiah of Isaiah 53.

In the time of God’s favor He answered the Servant and will make him a covenant for the people, restoring the land’s desolate inheritances. Paul quotes this: “Now is the day of salvation.” Nephi’s version addresses it to “O isles of the sea.”

f.w: In an acceptable time have I heard thee

n: He will say to prisoners, “Come out,” and to those in darkness, “Show yourselves.” They’ll be like sheep grazing safely along the way home. Latter-day Saints also connect this to the spirit world and temple work.
They won’t hunger or thirst, nor be struck by desert heat, because the Merciful One leads them to springs of water. John uses this image for the redeemed in heaven.

f.w: They shall not hunger nor thirst

n: God will turn mountains into roads and raise up highways for the journey home.
They come from far away—north, west, and from Sinim. The location of Sinim is uncertain; many scholars think of Syene (Aswan) in southern Egypt.

f.g: Uncertain; the Dead Sea Isaiah Scroll reads “Syene” (Aswan, Egypt). Some older readers suggested China.

n: Heavens, earth, and mountains are told to burst into song because the Lord has comforted His people. Nephi’s version adds “for the feet of those who are in the east shall be established” and “they shall be smitten no more.”
But Zion complains, “The Lord has abandoned me and forgotten me.” Nephi’s version adds, “but he will show that he hath not.”
God answers with one of scripture’s tenderest images: can a nursing mother forget her baby? Even if she could, I will never forget you. God’s love is more faithful than a mother’s.

f.w: Can a woman forget her sucking child

n: God has engraved Zion on the palms of His hands. Christians and Latter-day Saints see here the nail wounds in the Savior’s hands—a permanent reminder of His people.

f.w: I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands
thy walls are continually before me
f.g: Like a builder’s plans always in view; God never stops thinking of rebuilding Zion.

n: Zion’s children hurry home, while those who destroyed her leave.

f.g: The Dead Sea Scroll and others read “your builders hurry.”

n: Look around! Your gathered children will adorn you like a bride’s jewelry. Gathered Israel is Zion’s beauty.
Ruined, empty places will become too crowded for all the people, and the oppressors will be far away.
Children born to bereaved Zion will say, “It’s too cramped here—make room for me!” A picture of explosive growth after near-extinction.

f.w: The place is too strait for me

n: Zion will wonder, “Where did all these children come from? I was alone, a captive wanderer!” The latter-day gathering surprises even Israel.

God will raise a signal to the Gentiles, and they will carry Israel’s sons and daughters home in their arms and on their shoulders. Nephi explained this as Gentile nations in the last days helping restore Israel and bringing them the gospel.

f.w: set up my standard to the people

f.g: A banner or flag raised as a rallying signal.

n: Kings and queens will care for Israel like foster parents and honor them, and Israel will know that those who wait on the Lord are never put to shame.

f.w: kings shall be thy nursing fathers
they shall not be ashamed that wait for me

n: A doubtful question: can prey be taken from a warrior, or captives rescued from a tyrant? It seems impossible. Nephi’s version reads “For shall the prey be taken from the mighty...”

f.g: Possibly “the captives of the righteous” or, by a small change, “of the tyrant.”

n: God’s answer: yes! He will fight against Israel’s enemies and save her children. Jacob, Nephi’s brother, quoted this passage as part of his great covenant sermon.

f.w: I will contend with him that contendeth with thee

n: Oppressors will turn on each other and destroy themselves. Then all humanity will know that the Lord is Israel’s Savior, Redeemer, and Mighty One of Jacob.

f.w: I the LORD am thy Saviour and thy Redeemer
